The actual variance difference is approximately \(0.0444902\), while the printed expression gives \(-0.3644902\). All masses are strictly positive and \(\mathbb ES=0\).

Appendix B.2 of f-Trajectory Balance gives the same sign through \(1-2f^{\prime}(u)\); setting \(f(u)=u\log u\) gives \(-1-2\log u\).

review-neurips-2026-150817.title: Smart Picks in the Dark: Towards Efficient RLVR for Reasoning via Tracing Metacognitive Pivots

checks.location: Appendix A.1, Proposition 1, Equations (10)-(11) and (26)
checks.claim: Under KL(old||new)<=delta the exact maximum improvement is at most sqrt(2 delta mu_old(1-mu_old)).
checks.explanation: The proof replaces the KL constraint and objective by local Taylor models, then treats their resulting optimum as an exact finite-update bound. The omitted higher-order terms can make the proposed upper bound too small, including for arbitrarily small asymmetric updates.
checks.demonstration:
Use a full-support Bernoulli policy with old success probability \(p=0.1\), new probability \(q=0.2\), binary reward equal to the output and old advantage \(R-p\). This is a smooth policy family with nonsingular Fisher information. Set the budget to the exact KL:

\[
\delta=\operatorname{kl}(0.1,0.2)
=0.1\log\frac{0.1}{0.2}+0.9\log\frac{0.9}{0.8}
\approx0.0366900140.
\]

The feasible update improves the surrogate by \(q-p=0.1\), but the claimed bound is

\[
\sqrt{2\delta(0.1)(0.9)}\approx0.0812662447<0.1.
\]

This is not only a large-step effect. For \(q=p+t\),

\[
\operatorname{kl}(p,p+t)=\frac{t^2}{2p(1-p)}+
\frac{(2p-1)t^3}{3p^2(1-p)^2}+O(t^4).
\]

For \(p<1/2\) and small positive \(t\), the negative cubic term again defeats the exact quadratic-only upper bound.
checks.repair: For \(0<p<1\), data processing through the success indicator gives \(\operatorname{kl}(p,q)\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{old}}\Vert\pi_{\mathrm{new}})\). Therefore the sharp positive-improvement bound is \(q_\delta-p\), where \(q_\delta\geq p\) solves \(\operatorname{kl}(p,q_\delta)=\delta\). The binary KL is increasing on \(q>p\), so this is a valid bound; reweighting the success and failure classes while preserving their conditional laws attains it. Alternatively retain the square-root expression explicitly as the optimum of the linear objective and quadratic Fisher constraint, rather than as an exact-KL inequality.
checks.scope: The source version corrects an earlier gradient sign but retains the finite-KL bound. The counterexample concerns that exact inequality; the quadratic Fisher-constrained optimum has its own local interpretation.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 1 bounds the exact maximum surrogate improvement for a binary reward under \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{old}}\Vert\pi_{\mathrm{new}})\leq\delta\), where \(p=\mu_{\mathrm{old}}(q)\).
checks.title: The Fisher approximation is not an exact finite-KL improvement bound
checks.whyItMatters: The instantaneous utility can remain a useful local variance proxy, but its stated exact maximum and consequences relying on exactness are not established.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix A.1, Proposition 1, Eqs. (10)–(11) and (26) (arXiv v2)

tokenpb-average-calibration-guarantee.title: TokenPB: Enabling VLA Action Self-Verification via VLM Token Probability Bucketing
tokenpb-average-calibration-guarantee.summary: Mean calibration error does not guarantee correct ranking at every observation, and the Gibbs utility bound omits the score-to-utility scale. Two additional gaps concern transferring fixed-length sequence-ranking and properness results to scores and losses normalized by each sequence’s own length.

checks.location: AppendixC.5 equivalence sentence line1196; Section4.2 score and AppendixG.4 own-length normalization
checks.claim: Sequence log-probability ordering is equivalent to the implemented mean-token-log-likelihood ordering.
checks.explanation: Dividing negative log scores by different positive lengths can reverse their order. The fixed-length appendix theorem is correct, but it does not provide this variable-length equivalence.
checks.demonstration: Take two positive sequence probabilities \(\pi(c_1)=0.45\) and \(\pi(c_2)=0.35\), with lengths one and two, leaving probability \(0.20\) for other sequences. Sequence probability prefers \(c_1\). The mean log scores are approximately \(-0.799\) and \(-0.525\), so the normalized rule prefers \(c_2\). A prefix-free autoregressive realization can assign these sequence masses, so the example is consistent with sequence probabilities.
checks.repair: For the stated sequence-ranking guarantee, use summed log probabilities or restrict all compared candidates at each observation to the same positive token length. Under the latter condition, division by the common L is a positive scaling and preserves every ordering. If mean-token likelihood is the intended objective for varying lengths, formulate the quality-alignment and calibration assumptions for that score instead of importing the sequence theorem.
checks.scope: A transfer gap between the valid fixed-length theory and the variable-length scoring rule. It is not a counterexample to the theorem under its explicit common-L convention.
checks.title: Sequence ranking needs a length condition before transfer to mean-token scores
checks.claimContext: Appendix C.1 fixes a common sequence length L and analyzes sequence log probabilities. The main scoring rule and Appendix G.4 divide each candidate’s log probability by its own token count. The paper transfers the sequence-level ranking result to that variable-length score.
checks.verificationNote: The relevant assertions were checked against arXiv:2603.18091v2, uploaded 2026-10-12, and the saved independent mathematical assessment. The appendix’s fixed-length result is correct; the retained issue is its transfer to the variable-length score or loss.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 4.2 scoring; Appendix C.1 fixed-length setup; Appendix G.4 inference score

checks.location: Section4.3 line190; co-training loss in Section4.2 line179 and Algorithm1; compare AppendixC.2
checks.claim: The actual length-normalized bucket loss is strictly proper for the expert sequence distribution P*.
checks.explanation: Outcome-dependent inverse-length weights change the population optimum. Properness of each conditional token score does not remove those example weights.
checks.demonstration: Let \(a_c=P^*(c)/L(c)\). On the probability simplex, a Lagrange multiplier gives the unique positive-probability optimum \[q^*(c)=\frac{a_c}{\sum_d a_d}=\frac{P^*(c)/L(c)}{\sum_dP^*(d)/L(d)}.\] For \(P^*=(0.45,0.35,0.20)\) and lengths \((1,2,2)\), this is \((0.62069,0.24138,0.13793)\), not \(P^*\). Its weighted loss is about \(0.66146\), versus \(0.70399\) at \(P^*\).
checks.repair: Use summed sequence NLL to recover strict properness for \(P^*\), or assume the length is constant conditional on the observation. Alternatively, explicitly define the inverse-length-reweighted target above; the objective is a positive scalar multiple of its cross-entropy, hence strictly proper for that target. The subsequent quality-alignment argument must then refer to the reweighted distribution.
checks.scope: The valid unweighted Proposition C.2 is retained. The error is its transfer to the variable-length training objective; no claim is made that a trained checkpoint attains the displayed population optimum.
checks.title: Inverse-length weighting changes the sequence distribution learned by the loss
checks.claimContext: Proposition C.2 correctly proves strict properness of unweighted sequence log loss. Section 4.3 applies that conclusion to the actual per-sequence loss divided by the demonstration’s own length.
checks.verificationNote: The relevant assertions were checked against arXiv:2603.18091v2, uploaded 2026-10-12, and the saved independent mathematical assessment. The appendix’s fixed-length result is correct; the retained issue is its transfer to the variable-length score or loss.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 4.2 normalized objective; Section 4.3 properness claim; Appendix C.2

checks.location: DefinitionC.3 Eq.13 and TheoremC.5 proof Eq.16 (lines1172,1190-1212)
checks.claim: Mean-over-observations maximum log calibration error below half the minimum positive gap guarantees correct ranking at every observation.
checks.explanation: A small mean can hide a large error on a rare observation. The proof’s valid triangle inequality needs the pointwise error, not its expectation.
checks.demonstration: Write \(e(s)=\max_m|\log\pi_m(s)-\log P_m^*(s)|\). The valid bound is \(\log\pi_i(s)-\log\pi_j(s)\geq\gamma_{ij}(s)-2e(s)\). Take two states with probabilities \(0.96\) and \(0.04\), two one-token candidates, and \(P^*=(0.8,0.2)\) at both states. Let \(\pi=P^*\) at the common state and \(\pi=(0.4,0.6)\) at the rare state. Then \(\gamma_{\min}=\log4\), \(e_{\rm rare}=\log3\), and \[\varepsilon_{\rm cal}=0.04\log3\approx0.04394<\tfrac12\log4,\] yet the rare-state ranking is reversed. All probabilities are positive; a separate softmax logit for each state gives a realizable smooth model. Using one-token candidates removes any length ambiguity.
checks.repair: For literally every-state ranking, assume \(\sup_s e(s)<\gamma_{\min}/2\). An essential supremum instead yields an almost-sure statement. With the existing mean definition and a positive uniform ideal margin, any ranking failure implies \(e(s)\geq\gamma_{\min}/2\), so Markov gives \[\Pr(\text{any ranking failure})\leq\min\{1,2\varepsilon_{\rm cal}/\gamma_{\min}\}.\] This is the probabilistic guarantee supported by the original average.
checks.scope: The universal ranking guarantee is false under mean calibration. Local scoring monotonicity, summed-loss properness and empirical action-selection performance are separate.
checks.whyItMatters: Theorem C.5’s universal ranking guarantee does not follow from its mean calibration premise. The example does not show that every prediction is unreliable or that the reported robotics improvements disappear.
checks.title: Mean calibration does not guarantee every observation’s ranking
checks.claimContext: If mean log-space calibration error is below half the minimum positive ideal log-probability gap, the verifier ranks every candidate pair correctly at every observation.
checks.verificationNote: The relevant assertions were checked against arXiv:2603.18091v2, uploaded 2026-10-12, and the saved independent mathematical assessment. The final scope and grade distinguish the demonstrated local mathematical issue from untested downstream claims.
checks.checkedLocation: Definition C.3, Equation (13); Theorem C.5, Equations (15)–(16)

checks.location: AppendixD.2 PropositionD.2 Eq.23 and proof Eq.24-25; main Section4.3 Eq.4
checks.claim: Gibbs selection on calibrated log sequence probabilities has Q-regret bounded by logM/lambda+LQ*epsilon_cal from scoring monotonicity.
checks.explanation: The Gibbs inequality controls regret in the units of the score in its exponent. Monotonicity, even exact positive affine alignment, does not make those units equal to utility units.
checks.demonstration: Use one state, three one-token candidates, perfect calibration \(P^*=\pi=(0.36,0.34,0.30)\), and \(\lambda=12\). Define \[Q_i=\frac{\log(P_i^*/0.30)}{\log(1.2)},\] so \(Q=(1,0.686497,0)\in[0,1]^3\) is an increasing affine function of the log score with slope \(L_Q=1/\log(1.2)\). Gibbs probabilities are approximately \((0.618891,0.311696,0.069413)\), giving utility regret \(0.167131\). The printed bound is \(\log3/12\approx0.091551\), since calibration error is zero. The actual score regret \(0.0304715\) satisfies its Gibbs bound; converting it to utility multiplies it by \(L_Q\).
checks.repair: Assume explicitly that \(Q=f(\log P^*)\) for a nondecreasing \(L_Q\)-Lipschitz function. If the candidate log-score error at state s is bounded by e(s), the Gibbs score bound and two triangle inequalities give utility regret at most \(L_Q[\log M/\lambda+2e(s)]\). Averaging gives \(L_Q[\log M/\lambda+2\varepsilon_{\rm cal}]\). Alternatively, define the Gibbs temperature in utility units and prove the required utility calibration directly.
checks.scope: This is a finite-temperature Gibbs-surrogate bound, independent of the mean-versus-pointwise error and of token lengths. It does not refute the reported deterministic argmax inference rule.
checks.title: The Gibbs utility bound omits the score-to-utility scale
checks.claimContext: Appendix D.2 samples with Gibbs weights based on log sequence probabilities, then states regret in utility Q using the same temperature. The proof allows an affine relationship between ideal log score and Q but does not carry its slope into the entropy term.
checks.claimFormula: \mathbb E[Q(a^*\mid s)-Q(a^{\rm sel}\mid s)]\leq\frac{\log M}{\lambda}+L_Q\varepsilon_{\rm cal}
checks.verificationNote: The relevant assertions were checked against arXiv:2603.18091v2, uploaded 2026-10-12, and the saved independent mathematical assessment. The final scope and grade distinguish the demonstrated local mathematical issue from untested downstream claims.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix D.2, Equations (22)–(25); Section 4.3 expected-selection bound
